title: Knight Outposts
subtitle: Park a knight where no pawn can ever kick it.
goals: Trade defenders to own the square

steps.say: An OUTPOST is a square in enemy territory that no enemy pawn can ever attack — ideally protected by one of your own pawns. A knight on an outpost is a permanent thorn: it can't be traded cheaply, can't be kicked, and radiates threats forever. Finding outposts is what separates positional players from move-to-move players.

steps.prompt: Black has no c-pawn and no e-pawn. One square in their camp is an eternal home for your knight — find it!
hints: Which square could a black pawn NEVER attack? Check what pawns Black is missing.
d5: black's c- and e-pawns are gone, and your e4 pawn protects it. Forever.

line.say: The eternal knight! Protected by your pawn, unreachable by any black pawn until the end of time. From d5 it dominates e7, c7, f6, b6 — Black must play the whole game around it.

rejections.say: a6! and the knight is kicked straight back. b5 can be attacked by a black pawn, so it was never an outpost — just a visit. d5 is the PERMANENT address.

steps.wrongSay: The outpost is a square Black's pawns can never touch, guarded by yours. Look at the hole where Black's c- and e-pawns used to be.
steps.successSay: Missing enemy pawns leave permanent holes. The knight is the piece that moves in.

steps.prompt: Switch sides! White's knight is eyeing the d5 hole. You're Black — deny the outpost before it exists!
hints: An outpost only exists if your pawns can never attack it. Which of your pawns can still cover d5?
Either the c-pawn or the e-pawn can take control of d5 — one modest step.

line.say: Denied! Now Nd5 simply loses the knight to exd5. One quiet pawn move and the 'eternal knight' plan dies before it was born. This is called prophylaxis.
The square is covered — Nd5 would now be met by cxd5. Grandmasters make these quiet denials constantly; amateurs notice the knight only after it lands.

rejections.say: Nd5! The eternal knight arrives while you nudged a wing pawn. One prophylactic move — e6 or c6 — would have denied the square forever.

steps.wrongSay: White wants Nd5 permanently. Which pawn move takes that square away for good?
steps.successSay: Preventing your opponent's dream square is worth as much as finding your own.

steps.prompt: You want the d5 outpost — but Black's f6 knight guards it. Remove the defender, then move in!
hints: Count the fighters for d5: your knight wants in, their knight keeps it out. Eliminate it!
Your bishop can capture the f6 knight right now — then d5 has no defenders left.

line.say: ...and the knight takes the throne — attacking the f6 bishop on arrival! A bishop traded for an eternal knight on d5 is a trade masters make happily.

rejections.say: Nxd5! exd5 — the knights are traded and your 'outpost' is now just a pawn. Fine, but the ETERNAL KNIGHT was the prize: remove the defender first with Bxf6.

steps.wrongSay: d5 is contested by the f6 knight. What removes that knight from the equation?
steps.successSay: Outpost strategy in full: find the square, remove its defenders, occupy forever.

steps.prompt: Your d5 knight has watched long enough. Black's queen and rook stand on its jump squares — feast!
hints: List the knight's jumps from d5 and check each for enemy pieces and defenders.
b6: attacks BOTH the a8 rook and the d7 queen — and no black pawn covers b6 (the a- and c-pawns are gone!).

line.say: The outpost pays out! Queen and rook forked from a square nothing defends...
The rook is yours. THIS is why eternal knights win games: sooner or later, the fork appears.

rejections.say: Qxe7! The queen was guarding e7 — your beautiful knight died for a check. The UNDEFENDED fork square was b6.
gxf6 — the pawn simply eats your knight. A sac needs a follow-up; the quiet monster-jump to b6 forked queen and rook for free.

steps.wrongSay: The knight has a fork available — on the one jump square no black piece or pawn defends.
steps.successSay: Outposts are investments; forks are the dividend. Patience, then profit.
